title: Wash, and be clean (2 Kings 5:1–14)
hook: the general wanted something grand, and was told to wash in the Jordan

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shunammite built a small room for a stranger and turned down a favor at court: I dwell among my people. Did you make a little room for someone? Today, someone arrives at Elisha's door with horses and chariots. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

Horses, chariots, servants, and gifts of silver, gold and fine clothing. Naaman, captain of the army of the king of Aram, has come a long way, and he has come in style. The text calls him a great man, honored by his king, a mighty man of valor. And then it adds a short phrase that undoes all of it: he was a leper. He has a skin disease no rank can cure. Someone has told him there's a prophet in Israel who could heal him. So the whole procession pulls up and stops at Elisha's door. And Elisha doesn't come out.
screen: `HORSES, CHARIOTS, SILVER, GOLD.` → `A GREAT MAN, BUT A LEPER.` → `ELISHA DOESN'T COME OUT.`

segments.voice: Instead, Elisha sends a messenger with a short instruction: go and wash in the Jordan seven times, and your flesh will be restored, and you will be clean. That's it. No ceremony. No prophet at the door. Naaman is furious, and the text lets us hear exactly why. He says, in effect: I thought he would surely come out to me, stand there, call on the name of his God, wave his hand over the spot, and heal me. He had pictured the whole scene in advance. And then the insult of the river itself. Are not Abana and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn't I wash in them and be clean? He turns and leaves in a rage. What stops him is not the prophet. It's his own servants. They come near and call him, my father. If the prophet had asked you to do some great thing, wouldn't you have done it? "How much rather then, when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?" It's a sharp, kind question. Naaman was ready for difficulty. He was ready for a quest, a price, a drama worthy of a general. What he couldn't accept was something ordinary. A plain river. Seven dips. No prophet at the bank. And yet he goes down to the Jordan, dips himself seven times, just as the man of God said, and his flesh comes back like the flesh of a little child, and he is clean. Notice the turn. The cure was there from the first message. What stood in the way was Naaman's picture of how it should happen. The hard part wasn't the washing. It was getting down off the chariot.
screen: `GO AND WASH IN THE JORDAN.` · `I THOUGHT HE WOULD COME OUT.` · then, large: `WASH, AND BE CLEAN.` · then: `LIKE THE FLESH OF A LITTLE CHILD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try the simple thing. Uncross your arms and breathe out slowly. Then name something you've been stuck on, waiting for a big solution: a tense relationship, a messy room, a health habit, a project you can't start. Now ask what Naaman's servants asked: if the answer were something grand, would I do it? Then what's the plain, ordinary step I keep stepping over? An apology. Ten minutes of tidying. A walk. A glass of water. A phone call. Name it to yourself. Then take that first step in your mind: down off the chariot. The bell holds the time.
Wash. The plain instruction a great general almost refused: go down into an ordinary river and dip, as the prophet said. Today's word.
Your line: wash, and be clean. Today, when you catch yourself waiting for a grand fix, try the simple thing first. Day seven hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Jews read Naaman's healing as part of the book of Kings and as a haftarah alongside the Torah's laws of skin disease, which are read in the book of Leviticus.

fork.setup: you're Naaman. the prophet won't even come to the door, and says to wash in the Jordan. what do you do?
options: go home to the rivers of Damascus.
listen to your servants and wash.
fork.reveal: he turns away in a rage, but his servants reason with him. he washes, and his flesh is restored.

original.note: Hebrew: wash, and be clean, the servants' words in 2 Kings 5:13.

trapdoor: what you thought: a magic river.
what it means: the cure was simple from the start; Naaman's pride had to come down first.
what a scholar hears: Naaman scripted the miracle in advance: I thought, he will surely come out to me.

notes: Auditor (2026-10-01): practice opening varied to break the "Settle and breathe. Bring to mind" template.
Editor: cut the word count ('three words'; KJV 5:1 reads 'but he was a leper'); removed unsupported 'gently', 'muddy' and 'nobody watching' (his servants were there); practice wording varied.
Verify KJV wording at 2 Kings 5:13; JPS 1917 may differ slightly ('Wash, and be clean' is shared).
Naaman's speech (5:11–12) and the servants' first line (5:13) are paraphrased close to KJV without quotation marks; the trapdoor's 'I thought, he will surely come out to me' is near-KJV.
'Seven times' is stated in 5:10 and 5:14 and kept because the cited text says it.
The person who told Naaman about the prophet (the captive girl, 5:2–3) is left vague on purpose; she is tomorrow's lesson.
howItsDone: confirm 2 Kings 4:42–5:19 as the haftarah for Tazria; 'Aram' follows the Hebrew where KJV has 'Syria'.
'leper' follows KJV; the Hebrew tzara'at is a skin affliction, not necessarily modern leprosy.
